title: Towards Fairness under Label Bias in Image Segmentation: Impact, Measurement and Mitigation
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Label error is measured by comparing labels to confident predictions, splitting disagreement into excess and deficit, then combining them into summary scores.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed arrows between titled stages, confusion matrix center
description: A three-stage figure read left to right. Each stage has a light-blue title tab (Comparison, Decomposition, Assembly), and dashed arrows connect the tabs. The left panel shows a dark blob-shaped segmentation mask for the observed label and another for the model's confident prediction. Next to them are an overlay of the two masks with orange and blue fringes, a pixel-grid overlay, and a legend for agreement, excess and deficit. The middle panel is a 2x2 confusion matrix of observed label against CL prediction. Its cells are background agreement (gray), deficit (blue), excess (orange) and foreground agreement (navy). A caption says only off-diagonal pixels contribute to label error. The right panel has three rows. Excess + Deficit gives total error (LER). Excess − Deficit gives error direction (DR), drawn with a double-headed arrow. A ratio RR compares a biased group with a reference group. Formulas sit at the right of each row. The eye goes first to the orange and blue blocks and the colored matrix.
caption: CL-based decomposition of annotation disagreement. Observed labels \(y_{\mathrm{obs}}\) are compared with confident assignments derived from cross-fitted model predictions.
abstract: Biases in annotation pipelines may introduce label bias: when annotation quality or style varies systematically across demographic subgroups, causing disparities in performance and auditability. Label bias in image segmentation remains underexplored, as even detecting it typically requires clean, unbiased annotations, which are not readily available. We present a Confident Learning framework adapted to segmentation for auditing label bias directly in the training data without a clean, unbiased ground truth. By comparing the provided training labels to the model's confident predictions, we measure the prevalence and direction of suspected label errors; where standard overlap metrics like Dice fail. We further show that label bias influences subgroup separability in the encoder's feature space, an artifact we leverage for bias mitigation rather than suppressing it. We evaluate three datasets spanning from synthetic to real-life bias and across experimental conditions, showing how our framework produces proxy audit signals without clean labels and mitigates disparities with a correctly identified cleaner reference group.
